title: Who is poor
hook: the poor person isn't the one with too little but the one who craves more

segments.voice: Yesterday: nowhere and everywhere, the plant moved too often. Your line was go deep. Did you read one thing twice? Day four hundred thirty-four. The end of a week.

Ask a friend how much money would make them feel secure, and remember the number. Ask again five years and two raises later. Quite often the number has moved, and it is still a little more than they have. The target walks away as they walk toward it. Seneca would not have been surprised. At the end of his second letter, after telling Lucilius to stay with a few good authors, he hands him a small gift, a thought he picked up that day, and then gives it a twist that sticks. Today: Epicurus.
screen: `HOW MUCH WOULD BE ENOUGH?` → `ALWAYS A LITTLE MORE.` → `WHO IS POOR.`

segments.voice: First, the gift. Seneca says he's been reading Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, and found this: contented poverty is an honorable thing. Seneca likes it, but he pushes it one step further. If it's contented, he says, it isn't really poverty at all. Second, the turn. Then his own line. The poor person isn't the one who has too little. It's the one who craves more. What does it matter, he asks, how much someone has locked in the safe or stored in the barn, how many flocks or how much interest, if they're always eyeing what belongs to someone else and counting what they don't have yet? Third, the limit. So what is the right measure of wealth? First, Seneca says, to have what is necessary. Then, to have what is enough. Not a fixed number. A line you draw yourself. Fourth, the honest note. Seneca wrote this as a very rich man, and Tacitus records a critic in Seneca's own lifetime attacking him for that wealth. We'll come back to that gap. But the idea doesn't depend on the man. Look at the week we've walked: peace of mind, the pond unstirred; attention; thank you, teacher, at the Discourses' close; then Seneca's letters: dear friend, hold this hour, go deep, and now crave less. Different days, one thread. And Seneca's point, once more: whoever keeps counting what they don't have yet is poor, whatever is in the safe.
screen: `EPICURUS: CONTENTED POVERTY.` · `POOR IS THE ONE WHO CRAVES MORE.` · `FIRST NECESSARY, THEN ENOUGH.` · `THE WEEK: ONE THREAD.` · then, large: `CRAVE LESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wanting: new shoes, a bigger place, a gadget, a little more in the account. Picture it clearly. Now ask Seneca's two questions. Is it necessary? And if not, would I already have enough without it? Don't force an answer. Just let the want get a little smaller, the way a balloon softens when you let out some air. Breathe. Notice what you already have, right here, that's enough for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Epicurus. The rival philosopher Seneca was reading: his line that contented poverty is honorable, which Seneca pushes further, since the poor person is the one who craves more.
Your line: crave less. The next time you catch yourself wanting something today, ask whether you already have enough, and let the want shrink one size. Day four hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism ask whether a desire is necessary or merely more, and set their own limit of enough instead of chasing a moving target.

original.script: non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit, pauper est
original.say: non kwee PA-rum HA-bet, sed kwee ploos KOO-pit, POW-per est
original.note: Latin: not the one who has too little, but the one who craves more, is poor.

trapdoor: what you thought: poor means not much money.
what it means: Seneca says poverty is craving more; the measure of wealth is first what's necessary, then what's enough.
what a scholar hears: the line answers a saying of Epicurus; Tacitus records the senator Suillius attacking Seneca's great fortune while Seneca was alive.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): cut 'repeated ever since', 'one of the richest men in Rome' and 'hypocrite'; Seneca's wealth now attributed to Tacitus, Annals 13.42 (Suillius); replaced the generic closing line with Seneca's own point from 2.6; 'often closes early letters' narrowed to letter two.

Letter 2.5–6: Epicurus' 'honesta res est laeta paupertas'; Seneca's reply that contented poverty is not poverty; 'non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit, pauper est'; the measure of wealth 'primus habere quod necesse est, proximus quod sat est'. Paraphrased (Gummere wording not quoted because year-one writers could not verify it). Confirm.
Criticism of Seneca's wealth in his lifetime: Publius Suillius' attack (Tacitus, Annals 13.42). Confirm.
Week-end look-back (days 428–434): peace of mind, attention, thank you, teacher, dear friend, hold this hour, go deep, crave less.
Year two day 486 ('True riches') also uses this line; this day keeps the Epicurus exchange and the 'necessary, then enough' measure.
